Instead of relying on the upstream to carry the quarter, the Texas-based company showed that its refining and fuels business can swing the earnings picture in a matter of months. Adjusted earnings were higher than in the prior quarter, operating cash flow was robust, and net debt continued to fall as the balance sheet strengthened further. The release, issued recently, arrives at a moment when energy markets are still processing geopolitical disruption, uneven demand signals and a more cautious tone about the path of crude benchmarks. Readers following oil and gas stocks will recognise that the quarter's story is less about the direction of oil prices than about how a large, diversified operator turns operational reliability into cash. The headline takeaway from the release is a change in the centre of gravity. For several years, the narrative around Exxon Mobil focused on upstream growth, with Guyana and the Permian Basin supplying most of the excitement. In the latest quarter, the energy products division, which houses refining and fuels, produced earnings that more than doubled from the previous quarter and outpaced the upstream segment by a clear margin. That reversal matters because it illustrates why integrated oil companies exist. When crude prices soften, refiners often benefit from cheaper feedstock, provided product prices keep. The company highlighted that crude unit utilisation at its Gulf Coast refineries reached full capacity during the period, alongside strong diesel output. Running plants at that intensity is rarely accidental. It reflects years of maintenance planning, unit upgrades and a deliberate effort to shift yields toward higher-value products such as distillates. The Beaumont refinery expansion is part of that story. The addition of capacity at the Texas site has lifted distillate production along the Gulf Coast meaningfully since the end of the last decade, giving the company more exposure to a product that remains tightly linked to freight, farming and industrial activity. The upstream segment posted lower adjusted earnings than in the previous quarter. Several factors explain most of the move. Lower realised prices weighed on revenue, and an accelerated entitlement effect in Guyana reduced the company's share of production under the terms of the production sharing contract. Entitlement mechanics can confuse casual observers. Under many production sharing agreements, the host government and partners recover costs first, and as those costs are repaid the operator's share of barrels can shift. The accelerated effect in the latest quarter means a portion of the expected shift arrived earlier than modelled, which trims posted earnings without changing the physical flow of oil from the Stabroek block. Despite the sequential decline, the longer-run upstream picture remains favourable on a year-to-date basis. Chemical products earnings declined in the quarter as margins narrowed, even though volumes in Asia Pacific improved. That combination is typical of a commodity chemical cycle in which new capacity in one region pressures pricing while demand growth remains uneven. The segment has been a source of frustration for the sector for some time, and the latest result does not change the tone. Year to date, however, the chemicals business is stronger than it was a year earlier. The company attributes that to record reliability and a wider feedstock advantage in North America, where abundant natural gas liquids give domestic crackers a cost edge over naphtha-based competitors in other regions. The company supports that view by pointing to cumulative structural cost savings that now run to many a substantial sum compared with the end of the last decade, with further savings added this year. Structural savings differ from cyclical ones because they persist when prices change. Examples include portfolio simplification, procurement reforms, digital tools and the reduction of duplicate functions. Whether the savings can continue to grow is an open question, because early gains are generally easier than later ones, and inflation in services and equipment can erode headline reductions. title: IMF Projects 22.3% GDP Growth For Guyana As ExxonMobil's (NYSE: XOM) Uaru Project Unlocks New Supply Capacity - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 5, 2026 | Economy & Business, Energy, Featured, News & Analysis Few economies anywhere in the world are expanding at the pace Guyana is, with the International Monetary Fund projecting GDP growth of 22.3% for the country in 2026. The driver behind that extraordinary figure is an oil sector that has transformed this small South American nation into one of the most closely watched energy stories on the planet. Guyana is closing in on a production milestone of one million barrels per day, a threshold that would have seemed unimaginable for the country just a decade ago. Adding further momentum to that trajectory is ExxonMobil’s (NYSE: XOM) Uaru project, which is expected to bring an additional 250,000 barrels per day of production capacity online. That incremental supply is significant not just for Guyana’s economy, but for energy markets that are increasingly anxious about concentration risk in global oil flows. Tensions across the Middle East have renewed concerns about the security of shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most critical chokepoints for crude oil transit. A disruption to that corridor would send shockwaves through energy markets, tightening supply precisely when major economies are already navigating inflationary pressures and uneven growth. Guyana’s expanding export capacity offers a geographically distinct alternative, with Atlantic Basin crude routes that bypass the vulnerabilities associated with Gulf shipping lanes entirely. The diversification argument has gained traction among energy analysts and policymakers who view Western Hemisphere production growth as a structural buffer against Middle Eastern supply shocks. For Guyana itself, the stakes extend well beyond barrels and benchmarks, with oil revenues reshaping public finances, infrastructure investment, and the country’s longer-term development outlook. The IMF’s 22.3% growth forecast places Guyana in a category virtually alone among its peers, reflecting how rapidly petroleum receipts are flowing into the broader economy. Exxon’s continued capital commitment through projects like Uaru signals that the investment cycle driving this boom still has considerable runway ahead, with capacity expansions compounding on one another. Whether Guyana’s institutions can manage that pace of wealth accumulation responsibly remains an open question, but the near-term production picture points firmly upward. For global energy markets contending with supply uncertainty, the emergence of a credible, scalable Atlantic producer may prove to be one of the more consequential developments of the decade. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

title: Is Exxon Mobil Stock Still Worth Owning After Its Quarter? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Shares of Exxon Mobil (XOM) rose 2.2% on October 30, 2026, the day it reported fiscal Q3 2026 results, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8%. The stock retreated by November 4, trading 7.6% below its close on the eve of the report. Shareholders own Exxon for profits and payouts that endure through the oil cycle, and its profit just jumped. So is that higher profit Exxon’s own, or the market’s? So far, more of it looks like the market’s. Exxon earned $15.4 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, against $7.55 billion a year earlier. The company earned $4.18 billion in fiscal Q1 2026, meaning the whole step up arrived in the last two quarters. Fiscal Q2 2026 profit was already $14.5 billion. Management said a lack of supply led to tight markets and higher prices. Its guess was that fuel markets would not get back closer to normal until well through 2027, or longer. Chevron and ConocoPhillips shares rose by similar amounts on report day, so the quarter did little to set Exxon apart from its peers. Exxon does have gains of its own. Management cited $16.9 billion of structural cost savings since 2019. Setting aside Middle East impacts, executives said production rose from a year earlier, helped by growth in the Permian and Guyana. Those savings accumulated over several years, while the higher profit has lasted just two quarters. Exxon’s payouts hold up so far. The company returned $9.4 billion to holders through dividends and buybacks in fiscal Q3 2026, against $18.5 billion of free cash flow. Management raised the dividend per share 4%, marking its 44th straight year of increases. The company also plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. Exxon carries light debt as well, at 4.9% of its market value against 19.2% for the S&P 500. Profit fell by more than a third, and the payouts kept going. Exxon earned $51.9 billion in the twelve months to September 2022, and $30.0 billion in the twelve months to September 2025. During that leaner year, free cash flow of $23.8 billion landed only a little above the $20.7 billion Exxon spent on buybacks alone. Total payouts of $37.9 billion ran well above free cash flow with $17.2 billion of dividends included. Management said that at the bottom of the cycle, Exxon does not pull back from its commitment to holders and uses the balance sheet to make up the difference. The company has less cash to draw on now, holding $12.2 billion at the end of September 2026, against $30.4 billion four years earlier. Apart from buybacks, management left its 2027 plan to a later date. The company said it will confirm key 2027 planning figures in a press release later in fiscal Q4 2026, offering more detail on its fourth-quarter call in January. Cash flow covered Exxon’s payouts in fiscal Q3 2026, while the company has held its higher profit for only two quarters. Its quarterly profit at the fourth-quarter report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch. Qualcomm (QCOM) CEO Cristiano Amon said its Starlink Mobile deal with Elon Musk’s SpaceX has “tremendous potential,” with deployment beginning in 2027 and the revenue opportunity expected to take shape more fully in fiscal 2028. SPCX stock fell nearly 4% on Wednesday, while QCOM jumped over 5% to its best day in over a month. This is a significant win for our infrastructure business and the beginning of a strategic relationship with tremendous potential,” Amon said on Qualcomm’s fourth-quarter earnings call on Wednesday. The partnership gives Qualcomm a role in powering Starlink Mobile’s upcoming nationwide terrestrial 5G network as the chipmaker expands beyond smartphones. As part of the deal, announced earlier Wednesday, SpaceX plans to deploy tens of thousands of sites. “Under a multi-year agreement, deployment begins in 2027, and it is expected to be one of the largest 5G deployments in the United States,” Amon said. While the rollout starts in 2027, Qualcomm expects revenue to begin appearing toward the end of its fiscal 2027, with the opportunity taking shape more fully the following fiscal year. “You should think about from a financial standpoint, it will start to appear as we exit fiscal 2027. It is more of a fiscal 2028 from a revenue standpoint,” Amon told on the call. Qualcomm will supply chips and foundational software through its Dragonwing infrastructure platforms, supporting the radios and processing equipment behind Starlink’s ground network. “We provide silicon content for radio, including massive MIMO, as well as the accelerator for the digital unit, and we provide software on the Layer 1,” Amon said. Starlink’s radios will use 64 transmit and 64 receive paths. Qualcomm said the tech can improve coverage and help the network carry more traffic over its available airwaves, while its platforms are designed to improve power efficiency. Amon also pointed to opportunities beyond the initial deployment, saying the partnership includes planning for the next generation of wireless. “I think we have seen a lot of trends of technology ranging from Open RAN to AI native as an opportunity to innovate in this space,” he said. The partnership supports SpaceX’s plans to combine ground-based cellular coverage with its satellite network. “Starlink is building the first fully-integrated nationwide satellite and terrestrial network that will keep people connected no matter where they are,” said Michael Nicolls, senior vice president of Starlink. SpaceX also agreed last month to acquire Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio, covering up to 14 megahertz of paired airwaves. For readers following US Oil and Gas Stocks, the results showed how the company's integrated model can perform in a volatile energy market. Geopolitical tension, including conflicts affecting energy supply, has pushed fuel prices higher this year. That backdrop supported refining profits, while the company's own cost discipline and project execution helped lift cash generation. The standout performer was the energy products segment, which includes refining. Earnings in this business more than doubled from the previous quarter, driven by higher margins and strong operations. Global refining utilisation reached a record, with US Gulf Coast crude units running close to full capacity. Refining profits tend to rise when fuel demand is strong and supply is tight. With gasoline and diesel prices elevated, ExxonMobil's large refining network was well positioned to benefit. Chemical product earnings declined as margins weakened, reflecting softer industrial demand and new global capacity. Specialty products, which include lubricants and base stocks, improved on better margins. Together, these segments show the diversity of the company's earnings base. Upstream earnings fell from the previous quarter, reflecting lower crude prices during the period and production entitlement effects in Guyana. Overall output stayed broadly stable. Even so, the long-term growth story in upstream remains strong. Guyana's Stabroek block surpassed a major cumulative production milestone just over a decade after discovery, described as the fastest ramp of any major offshore development. The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico also continued to deliver strong volumes. Management pointed to large structural cost savings achieved over recent years, which have strengthened earnings across commodity cycles. Automation is expanding in the Permian, with automated drilling rigs expected to cover a growing share of the fleet in coming years. The company also highlighted technology transfer between businesses. Refining expertise helped develop a lighter material used in drilling, an example of how integration can create advantages that standalone producers may lack. ExxonMobil is taking over operatorship of the Papua LNG project and increasing its stake, reinforcing its position in liquefied natural gas. LNG demand is expected to grow as countries look for cleaner alternatives to coal and secure energy supplies. In carbon capture, the company started another operation for an outside customer and gained approval for a new storage project. These businesses remain small but offer long-term options as industrial customers seek to reduce emissions. Strong cash flow supported continued dividends and share repurchases. The company is in its fifth decade of consecutive annual dividend increases and confirmed plans to keep repurchases at a similar pace next year. Net debt also declined during the quarter, strengthening an already solid balance sheet. This combination of rising dividends and repurchases is a key reason many income-focused investors follow the stock, particularly in a market where few large companies offer such a long payout record. ExxonMobil's strategy rests on investing in advantaged assets that remain profitable even when oil prices fall. Guyana and the Permian are central to that approach because they combine large resources with relatively low production costs. LNG projects add long-term contracted cash flows that are less sensitive to short-term price swings. Management has also emphasised capital discipline. Rather than spending heavily when prices are high, the company aims to keep investment steady and return excess cash to investors. That consistency has supported confidence in the dividend through several energy cycles. Refining and chemicals give the company a natural hedge. When crude prices fall, refining margins may improve because input costs drop, partly cushioning the impact on upstream earnings. This balance is a key reason large integrated companies are viewed as more resilient than pure producers. Energy prices remain volatile and tied to geopolitics, supply decisions by major producers and economic growth. Refining margins can fall quickly if demand weakens or new capacity arrives. Regulatory and climate policies also shape long-term investment decisions. As a heavyweight member of the NYSE Composite, ExxonMobil remains a bellwether for the US energy sector. The coming quarters will test whether refining strength persists and whether upstream growth in Guyana and the Permian continues on schedule. For now, the quarter highlights a company using its scale, integration and cost control to deliver solid results even as individual segments move in different directions. Low-cost production remains a focus across the portfolio. By concentrating capital on the most profitable barrels and steadily lowering break-even levels, ExxonMobil aims to keep generating cash even if prices fall sharply from current levels, a priority that management has repeated throughout the year. title: Will ExxonMobil's 100,000-BPD Diesel Expansion Boost Refining Profit? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is focusing on expanding its refining operations to increase the production of higher-value fuels, particularly diesel, and strengthen long-term profitability. The company expects its investments across U.S. refineries to increase distillate production by another 100,000 barrels per day (BPD). This expansion is part of XOM's broader strategy to improve its product mix and enhance earnings and cash flow. According to media reports citing ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods' Oct. 30, 2026, CNBC interview, the company plans to allocate approximately 10% of its more than $100 billion capital investment program for 2027-2030 toward refining operations, representing roughly $10 billion in planned spending. The integrated energy giant has already invested around $17 billion in refining since 2019, increasing crude processing capacity by nearly 10% over the period. Projects such as the Beaumont refinery expansion have contributed to a roughly 40% increase in U.S. Gulf Coast distillate production, while ongoing work at Baytown is aimed at expanding output. Beyond capacity additions, XOM has reduced refinery turnaround costs by about 30%, reflecting improved operational efficiency. The expansion comes as global refining capacity constraints have tightened fuel supplies and supported stronger refining margins. XOM's expanded trading and optimization capabilities allow it to secure advantaged feedstocks and direct refined products to higher-value markets. The planned increase in diesel production, combined with ongoing investments and improved operating efficiency, is expected to enhance ExxonMobil's earnings and cash flow, although profitability remains dependent on refining market conditions. The focus on increasing higher-value fuel production extends beyond ExxonMobil, with Valero Energy Corporation VLO and Marathon Petroleum Corporation MPC investing in refining efficiency and product optimization. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Valero Energy highlighted improvements in its product mix following the completion of the $230 million St. Charles refinery optimization project. Meanwhile, Marathon Petroleum emphasized that investments at its Garyville and Robinson facilities have enhanced operating flexibility and supported higher distillate yields. While VLO is working to strengthen its refining competitiveness through operational improvements, MPC remains focused on optimizing its refining network to support profitability.
